ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The gastrointestinal tract transforms food into nutrients, regulates fluid balance, and defends against pathogens. Clinicians must link symptoms to motility, secretion, absorption, and barrier function.

sections.p: The gut is a coordinated system of muscular, epithelial, and neural components that digest, absorb, and protect against microbes.
Food enters the stomach, mixes with acid and enzymes, moves to the small intestine where nutrients are absorbed, and residual material passes to the colon for water reabsorption and fecal formation.
Neural (vagal and sympathetic), hormonal (gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin), and local factors control motility and secretion.
Disorders arise from motility defects, secretion abnormalities, barrier dysfunction, or infection, leading to pain, malabsorption, bleeding, or systemic infection.
Symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, or weight loss require a systematic approach to identify underlying physiology derangements.
b: Weight loss suggests malabsorption or malignancy

t.b: Low Hb indicates bleeding or chronic disease

sections.p: Remember the sequence: ingestion → chewing → gastric mixing → small intestine absorption → colon water reabsorption. Link symptoms to each step.
b: Vomiting after meals points to gastric outlet obstruction or gastroparesis
Diarrhea with steatorrhea indicates pancreatic insufficiency

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for complications.
b: Proton pump inhibitors for acid-related disorders

sections.p: Differential diagnosis includes functional disorders and systemic diseases.
b: Functional dyspepsia vs peptic ulcer disease

sections.p: Normal fecal occult blood can miss right-sided lesions; low amylase may be seen in chronic pancreatitis.
b: Right-sided colon cancers may not bleed into stool

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, blood in stool, unexplained weight loss, fever with GI symptoms

faq.q: What causes chronic diarrhea in low-resource settings?
faq.a: Infections (Giardia, bacterial dysentery), malabsorption (celiac, tropical sprue), and parasitic infestations.

faq.q: How does HIV affect gut physiology?
faq.a: HIV damages gut-associated lymphoid tissue, leading to bacterial translocation, malabsorption, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

faq.q: Why is stool occult blood negative in some cancers?
faq.a: Right-sided colon cancers may bleed into the colon lumen and be digested before reaching stool, yielding a negative test.

exam: Explain how delayed gastric emptying can lead to postprandial nausea and weight loss.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a patient with steatorrhea.
Discuss the pathophysiological basis for abdominal pain in Crohn’s disease.
